### HTML scraping

We compared two versions of each webpage for binary claims classification. The first used paragraph text (`<p>`), and the second added visible headings (`<h1>`–`<h6>`). For each version, we built unigram TF-IDF features, fit PCA on the training pages, and used the resulting component scores in a logistic regression. We used five-fold cross-validation within the training set to select a common vocabulary-filtering rule and number of components. On the same 429 held-out webpages, adding headings increased accuracy from 77.39% to 78.09% (+0.70 percentage points) and ROC AUC from 0.8136 to 0.8332 (+0.0196).

### Bigrams

We formed bigrams from adjacent words within each paragraph, converted the bigram counts to TF-IDF features, and fit PCA on the training pages. A unigram logistic principal component regression model supplied predicted log-odds for a second-stage logistic regression. Each training page’s log-odds came from a model fit on the other folds. We compared a second-stage model using only those log-odds with one that also included the bigram component scores. On the same 429 held-out webpages, adding bigram components increased accuracy from 67.60% to 70.40% (+2.80 percentage points) and ROC AUC from 0.8109 to 0.8490 (+0.0381). This suggests that bigrams added predictive information beyond the word model on this split.

### Neural net

Our neural network model utilizes a feedforward network with 31570 inputs or predictors. These inputs originate from our training dataset, train_x, where each row represents an individual webpage, and its respective columns are the various word tokens and their TF-IDF values. Therefore, each input is simply the TF-IDF score for that specific token column. With regard to our single hidden layer, it has a unit size of 10, meaning every predictor is combined into 10 groups with various weights, and utilizes a hyperbolic tangent activation function, "tanh," to determine the contribution of each unit towards the output layer. It also possesses 315710 parameters, stemming from a combination of our unit number and amount of inputs, calculated by (unit number $\times$ input number + unit number), which in this case would be (10 $\times$ 31570 + 10 = 315710). We apply the same logic to the output layer, where it only has a unit size of 1, and therefore, its parameter number is (1 $\times$ 10 + 1 = 11), resulting in 315721 total parameters across both layers. In the final output, the sigmoid activation function is used to calculate the probability of the webpage containing relevant information, which is then used to determine the binary classification. Overall, our model is a relatively vanilla model. 

When configuring our model, we chose a binary cross-entropy loss function to minimize, "binary_crossentropy", and the optimization technique we decided to pair it with is stochastic gradient descent, "tf\$keras\$optimizers\$legacy\$SGD()." Through our testing on the training data, SGD did not perform well on lower epoch numbers, and as visualized in our graph, did not seem to improve the accuracy until close to 80 epochs, where there is an overall gradual increase. However, its progress stagnates after approximately 190 epochs, so we limit it to 200. A change of optimizer to "adam" was considered, but was ultimately discarded due to the massive difference between the training and validation accuracy. Its binary accuracies increased much faster than our SGD model, requiring fewer epochs to reach high values, but if too many were employed, the validation loss function would start increasing rather than our intended minimization. Additionally, despite having a much higher training accuracy, after 200 epochs, the "adam" optimizer would return a validation accuracy smaller in value than our SGD optimizer, so we decided to retain the SGD model. 

The results from our model on the validation set achieved a binary classification accuracy score of approximately 82.28%, only 4.3 percentage lower than the training accuracy. Compared to our task 1 accuracy score of 78.09%, obtained through principal component logistic regression with header information, our neural network performed about 4.2 percentage better in terms of binary classification.
